e922488474:
This chapter is about how a model chooses between tools, and how to write tools so that it chooses correctly. The tool definition (name, description, input schema, examples) is the only routing logic there is. So the chapter treats it as an API contract and covers:

  • what the model sees, and what it costs;
  • how overlap produces misrouting;
  • how to rename and split;
  • how the system prompt interferes;
  • what results should look like;
  • how to measure tool-selection accuracy with a harness you can run in CI.

A 12-tool support-agent case study goes from a catalogue that routes 25% of a labelled set correctly to one that routes 90%. Those numbers come from an offline proxy selector, not from Claude, and they carry the caveats that come with such numbers. Python and Java/Spring.
e441068c95:
A model chooses a tool by reading the text of every tool definition in the same context window as the conversation, so the name, description, parameter descriptions and examples are the whole routing logic: there is no classifier, router or keyword index behind them.

Therefore the work of tool design is to make each definition say what the tool is, when to use it, when not to, what it accepts and what it returns, to remove any overlap with its neighbours by expanding, renaming or splitting, to keep the system prompt from pulling selection toward a tool by keyword, and to prove the result with a labelled evaluation instead of an impression.
9e22900b1e:
Everything else follows.

The token cost of definitions exists because the text is resent on every request. Misrouting exists because two descriptions that read alike give the model nothing to separate them with.

The exam's advice follows the same way. Expand descriptions first, because the description is the strongest signal and the cheapest for you to change. Split generic tools, because one description can't carry five contracts. Review the system prompt, because "always start with X" is also text in the context, competing with the descriptions.
362a96700b:
The official task statement for 2.1 lists these knowledge points, and each is taught explicitly below:

  • tool descriptions are the primary mechanism the model uses to select a tool;
  • a good description includes input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundary explanations;
  • ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting (the official sample: get_customer chosen for order queries because both tools have minimal descriptions, and the first fix is to expand the descriptions);
  • system prompt wording can affect tool selection through keyword-sensitive instructions.

The skills are:

  • write descriptions that differentiate purpose, inputs, examples and boundaries;
  • rename tools and update descriptions to remove overlap;
  • split generic tools into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts;
  • review the system prompt for wording that creates unintended associations.
4b5c6b5efe:
A Spring developer should hold on to one analogy and one disanalogy.

The analogy: a tool definition is an API contract. The design principles that make a REST contract usable are the ones that make a tool usable: one resource per endpoint, precise types, explicit error cases, and documentation that states what the endpoint does not do.

The disanalogy: a REST client is a developer who reads your OpenAPI document once, thinks, and writes code. The consumer of a tool contract is a model. It rereads the contract on every single request and decides in one forward pass. It has no chance to ask you a question, and a dozen other contracts compete for the same decision. A contract that a human could puzzle out can still be unusable by a model.
83527b7567: Describing a callable interface precisely enough for a consumer who can't ask questions is an old problem. What changed in the last few years is that the consumer became a language model, and the quality of the description became the routing logic. The history explains why the exam's advice looks like API design advice. It is.
f0580fd67b:
Remote procedure call systems needed a way to describe an operation to a caller who hadn't seen the implementation. CORBA's IDL (early 1990s) described operations, types and exceptions in a language-neutral form, and stubs were generated from it. Web services repeated the move with WSDL (2001). UDDI tried to add discovery: a directory where a client could find a service by what it did. Telecom engineers know this from OSS/BSS integration, with SOAP interfaces and 400-line WSDLs.

Two lessons carry over. First, the type information was precise, but the human-readable documentation element was usually empty, because the consumer was a code generator that didn't read it. Second, discovery by description failed when the descriptions were thin.
d86cc78cfb:
Swagger (2011), later donated and renamed OpenAPI, made the REST contract machine-readable again, using JSON Schema for bodies. The ecosystem around it (springdoc, generated clients, contract tests) taught a generation of Java developers to treat the schema as the source of truth. It also taught them to ask four things of every endpoint: what does it accept, what does it return, what are the error cases, what is the example.

The same discipline applies to tools, with one difference. In OpenAPI, the description is for human readers and is often sloppy. In a tool definition, it's read by the consumer that makes the routing decision. So it can't be sloppy.
11ae213720:
MRKL Systems (Karpas et al., 2022) proposed routing a language model's requests to expert modules such as calculators and databases. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) put tool descriptions inside the prompt as text, and had the model write Action: Search[...] lines that a harness parsed. The quality of that paragraph decided whether the model picked the right tool. Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) trained a model to decide when to call an API. Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023) showed that retrieving the right API documentation made a large difference to call accuracy.

In June 2023, OpenAI shipped function calling. Anthropic's Messages API added tool use in 2024 with the same shape: a name, a description and an input_schema, with tool_use blocks coming back. Moving the definition into fields didn't change what the model does with it. It's rendered back into text, and selection is a language decision. What the fields did do was give the description and the schema separate jobs.
1c1bb329f3:
The Model Context Protocol (November 2024) standardised how tools reach a model application. One side effect: definitions are now often written by someone other than the person building the agent, and they arrive in bulk. The Claude docs describe a typical multiserver setup consuming tens of thousands of tokens of definitions.

The tooling followed in three directions:

  • more structure for arguments (strict tool use);
  • more guidance for the model (input_examples);
  • less context pressure (the tool search tool and defer_loading).

The tool search type string carries a date, tool_search_tool_regex_20251119, a hint that this area is moving. Check the docs for current names.
7fae9fa364:
Start from what the API actually does. You send a request with a tools array. The platform takes each definition, turns the array into a block of text, and places it in the prompt the model reads, alongside your system prompt and the conversation.

The Claude docs show the template. It's a short block that begins "In this environment you have access to a set of tools you can use to answer the user's question". It gives formatting instructions for calling the tools. It ends with "Here are the functions available in JSONSchema format", followed by your definitions. The exact internal rendering is not a contract and can change. What you can rely on is that the definition text is what the model sees.
7a64bdeeea:
The model then does what it does for every other token: it generates. If the best continuation is a call, it emits a tool_use block with a tool name and a JSON argument object, and the response ends with stop_reason: "tool_use".

That's the full mechanism. There's no URL pattern matcher, no index over names, no classifier trained on your tools. The name that appears in the block is the name the model judged the best fit, after reading the text.
a6e77ec815:
Two decisions are packed into that one block, and they're made from different parts of the definition.

  • The selection decision ("order_get_status rather than account_get_profile") is made mostly from the name and the description.
  • The argument decision ("order_id is ORD-118204, taken from the customer's sentence") is made mostly from the schema and the parameter descriptions. The description's sentence about input format helps too.

A tool can be chosen correctly and called with garbage, or chosen wrongly and called perfectly. Section 16 measures the selection decision on its own. The schema work of section 07 covers the second.
1cbd67bc72: The definition is the contract, and only the definition. Say a rule lives in your head, your wiki or your service code: "order ids start with ORD-", "this tool never changes data", "use the other tool for refunds". Then the model doesn't know it. It knows what's in the text.
f6e68a9af9: Everything in context competes. The system prompt, earlier turns, the results of earlier tool calls and the other tools' descriptions all influence the choice. Say the system prompt tells the agent to start every conversation by looking up the customer. That pulls toward the customer tool for order questions too. A tool result that contains the word "refund" can pull the next choice toward a refund tool.
0d58176e9a: Selection is probabilistic. Good definitions move selection accuracy a long way, but they don't make it exact. Where a wrong choice is unacceptable (a refund issued before identity verification), you add programmatic enforcement outside the model (chapter 03). For ordinary routing, fixing the definitions is the cheapest and most effective lever. That's why the exam lists it first.
9a1eceac58: A Spring analogy for the second point. Imagine a gateway with no routes. An operator reads each request, reads a page describing each backend in a few words, and decides. There's a sticky note on the desk: "always send people to customer service first". This gateway would fail the way tool selection fails. Backends with similar blurbs get confused, and the sticky note over-applies. Tool design is writing the blurbs so that this operator is rarely wrong.
2f34a97697: The name is read first, and must be reproduced exactly in the tool_use block. A name that states a resource and an operation (order_get_status) gives the model something to match against the user's words before it reads a description. A name like search or get_info says nothing, and everything falls on the description.
232356ad7a: The description. The Claude docs are blunt: "Provide extremely detailed descriptions. This is by far the most important factor in tool performance." They recommend "at least 3 to 4 sentences" per tool. They also list what a description should cover: what the tool does, when it should and shouldn't be used, what each parameter means, and caveats such as what the tool doesn't return. That list is the skeleton of section 06.
596fbf5b06:
The schema and parameter descriptions fix the shape of the call: types, required fields, enumerations, patterns, ranges, and a one-sentence format and default for each field. They drive the argument decision. They inform selection too: a property named order_id with the pattern ^ORD-\d{6}$ is further evidence about what the tool is for. Section 07 covers them.

Examples (input_examples, section 08) show concrete, well-formed calls, and help with optional parameters and formats.
290722296e:
A definition is read in company. The system prompt may contain instructions that mention tools, or the concepts they handle. The conversation history contains earlier tool calls and their results. If the previous result was a customer record, the model makes its next choice in the presence of that record.

None of this is configurable through the tool definition, but all of it changes the outcome. That's why the exam includes system prompt wording in 2.1, and why section 12 is devoted to it.
272d81a77a:
The API also lets you constrain the choice. tool_choice can be:

  • auto: the default with tools present; the model decides whether to call a tool, and which;
  • any: it must call one of the tools;
  • tool with a name: it must call that tool;
  • none.

The docs say that with any or tool, the API prefills the assistant message so no text precedes the tool_use block. They also say that changing tool_choice invalidates cached message blocks. At the time of writing, the define-tools page also says Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 reject any and tool, and recommends auto there; check the docs for your model. Chapter 06 covers tool_choice in depth.
59771a8632: Forcing a tool is not a substitute for good definitions. It removes the selection decision for one request. That's right in a few designed places, such as a step whose job is to emit one structured object. Everywhere else, it hides the routing problem. It also changes what an evaluation measures. With a forced tool there's nothing to evaluate, so the harness in section 16 uses auto.
dbc6c38228:
The definitions are resent as input on every request. So each character of a description is paid for on every call of every conversation. This doesn't argue for short descriptions. It argues for knowing the price, and spending it where it buys separation.

Example 01 (01_serialisation.py) measures it for the case-study catalogues. It uses an estimate of 3.5 characters per token for JSON. Calibrate with the count_tokens endpoint, which the example can call with --count.
38130514e4:
The full redesign with examples costs about 3,560 more tokens per request than the terse catalogue. At 5,000 requests a day, that's roughly 18 million extra input tokens a day for the definitions alone, before prompt caching.

Prompt caching changes the economics, because the tools array is part of the stable prefix. A cached prefix is read at a fraction of the normal input price, as long as you don't change the definitions or tool_choice between requests. (Check the pricing and caching docs for the current multiplier and the minimum cacheable length.)

That's a second reason to keep the catalogue stable, and to version it deliberately. An edit to any description invalidates the cached prefix for every conversation.
bd583e4c08:
Three consequences follow.

  • Measure before you trim: the ablation in section 17 tells you what a sentence buys.
  • Prefer a smaller catalogue of well-separated tools: every tool is a description to write, a look-alike pair to resolve, and a fixed cost per request.
  • For a large catalogue, stop sending most of the definitions (section 14) instead of compressing each one.
eb34513b5f: The exam's list for a good description has four items: input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundary explanations. The docs' list has four of its own: what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means, and caveats. Merged, they give eight parts. You won't need all eight on every tool. But for each tool, you should be able to say which ones you left out, and why.
5453665a18: The order is deliberate. Purpose is the line the model matches the request against. Use-when repeats the match in the user's own words. The boundary comes next, because it resolves ties between neighbours, and that's the exam's whole misrouting theme. The rest is about calling the tool well, not picking it.
2b8e6ea09d: Here's a typical first draft of the order tool, followed by what a review turns it into. The first draft isn't absurd. It's what most teams write on the first day:
035ad361ac:
Read it as the model does, with eleven other tools next to it. "Retrieves order details" doesn't say which details, for which requests, or what to do with a tracking number or an email. The free-form query forces the model to invent an input format on every call. And nothing separates this tool from get_customer, whose description says it retrieves customer information "by id, email, phone number or order number". An order number is now an input to two tools.

The review produces this:
6296c98d4b: Name the sibling in the boundary sentence. "Do not use it for X" gives a reason not to pick this tool. "Use Y instead" gives somewhere to go, and creates the cross-reference that example 06 looks for.
1537f511b3: Put side effects in the first sentence of a write tool. "This moves money and cannot be undone" makes the model prefer a read-only check first. It also signals your permission layer.
8c403ee2cc: Keep each tool's vocabulary distinctive, and keep persona and cross-tool workflow policy out of descriptions. Those belong in the prompt or a gate.
ceb498e96f: Do not ask for the model's reasoning in a parameter. The docs advise asking for an explanation, not reasoning. They note that reasoning-style parameters may trigger a refusal. A reason enum is fine; a chain_of_thought string is not.
af268ad81f:
The schema has three jobs. It tells the model what to put in each field. It lets you reject invalid calls before they do anything. And with strict tool use, it can constrain the model's output so that invalid calls aren't produced at all.

The example for this section is 03_input_schema_design.py. It runs six realistic bad inputs and one valid input against a lazy schema, and against the contract schema.
8371182d44: Five of the six bad inputs pass the lazy schema. All five would reach your business logic, and two of them (negative amount, missing idempotency key) would do damage there. Any Spring developer has seen this with a request DTO that lacks Bean Validation. There's one addition here: the caller is a model. It isn't trying to attack you, but now and then it will produce a plausible near-miss.
f3604f5f46: Required means required. Every optional parameter states its default in the description ("Page size, default 10"). An omitted optional is a decision made without seeing your code.
f00d07d413: Avoid either-or parameters. "Pass an email or a phone number" tempts the model to pass both, or neither. Use a discriminator: contact_type (enum) plus contact. If the inputs lead to different behaviour, they are two tools.
6a1802e15c: Avoid free-form catch-alls (query, data, params). They move the contract out of the schema and into the model's imagination. The linter in example 05 flags them first.
e66ce74169: Keep nesting shallow, set additionalProperties: false, and keep customer data and PHI out of the schema itself. The strict tool use docs warn that PHI must not appear in property names, enum values, const values or patterns, because schemas are cached.
9de71f3798:
Setting strict: true on a tool definition constrains the model's sampling, so that the tool name and input match the schema. The docs call it grammar-constrained sampling. Their motivating example is a passengers: int that might otherwise come back as "two".

Strict mode removes malformed calls. It doesn't make a call correct: a perfectly typed amount: 799.0 is still wrong for a refund over the limit. The define-tools page defers some details to other pages: supported JSON Schema keywords, strict-tool limits and model support. Check the docs before designing around a keyword.
d9d41c59c0: Whether or not you use strict mode, validate on the server. The harness is the boundary, and the model is not a trusted caller. The runtime in the companion code (tool_runtime.py) validates against the same schema before dispatch. It turns a violation into an is_error result that names the field and the allowed values:
b8f95527fe: That message is part of the interface. It says: nothing happened, here's the wrong field, here's what's allowed. Example 13 runs it. The model sends category: "limit" to ticket_escalate_to_human, receives the enum list, and retries correctly one turn later.
8d69f01e4a:
A schema says what is allowed. An example shows what is typical. input_examples is an optional array of example input objects on a tool definition. The docs say four things about it:

  • it helps with optional parameters, formats and complex nested inputs;
  • each example must be valid against the tool's input_schema, or the API returns a 400;
  • it applies to user-defined tools, not server-side ones;
  • it adds roughly 20 to 50 tokens per simple example, and 100 to 200 for complex nested ones.

The page we read names no beta header, and the installed Python SDK accepts the field on the ordinary tool type. Check the docs for your model and endpoint.
231c350c24: Choose examples that show what the schema can't express: that a status filter alone is a legitimate call, that since and limit go together, what a date looks like. Two or three per tool is enough. An invalid example fails the whole request, so lint them in CI (example 04):
f7a844ca86:
Two cautions.

First, examples leak. Whatever ids you put in them become part of what the model has seen. So never copy ids from your evaluation set (the test in example 19 fails the build if you do).

Second, examples are weak evidence for selection. In the ablation of section 17 they add 360 tokens and no first-call accuracy. That's expected: their value is in argument quality, which that metric doesn't measure.
60b28a38c6:
According to the define-tools page, the name must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$. Within that, the useful question is what the name lets the model infer before it reads a description.

The docs recommend meaningful namespacing. When tools span several services or resources, prefix the name with the service, as in github_list_prs and slack_send_message. They say this keeps selection unambiguous as the library grows, and that it matters especially with tool search.

The case study uses resource_verb_detail: order_get_status, billing_open_dispute, refund_issue. Grouping by resource keeps related tools adjacent. It lets a permission rule match billing_*, and it lets a regex search find the family.
5a34893080: Through MCP, the host composes the final name from the server and tool names. Claude Code exposes MCP tools as mcp__<server>__<tool> (check its docs for the current rule). So two servers that both export search become mcp__kb__search and mcp__orders__search. The prefix makes them unique, not different: both still say "search". Name tools as if the prefix weren't there, and name the server for the system it fronts (example 12).
d5984bcad5:
Tool names appear in many places: the system prompt, permission and allow rules, hook matchers, evaluation labels, dashboards and stored conversations. A rename done only in the definition leaves all of those pointing at nothing.

The safe pattern has three parts. Advertise only the new name to the model. Keep an alias table in the dispatcher and analytics. And update every place that names the tool in the same change.
f5702ca4dd:
The exam's sample scenario for 2.1, paraphrased: a production agent frequently calls get_customer when users ask about orders. Investigation shows that get_customer and lookup_order both have minimal descriptions and accept similar identifier formats. What is the most effective first step?

The expected answer is to expand each description with input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries. Replay the incident first, though. The mechanism is more useful than the answer.
a64b2a8018:
The first description is what happens when a team asks for a lookup that "works with whatever the customer gives us". The words "order number" are now in get_customer, so an order message matches it as well as it matches lookup_order. The system prompt adds "Always start by looking up the customer with get_customer before doing anything else".

Example 02 replays five order questions with the offline selector. Each line shows the pick, and the margin between winner and runner-up:
06c81cccbc:
Three of five go to the wrong tool. The two that go right win by 0.133 and 0.0, which is luck.

(The selector is a proxy, not Claude. The shape is what matters. A wrong pick with a large margin means the text actively pulls toward the wrong tool. A right pick with no margin means nothing pulls toward the right one.)

What the customer experiences is what makes this class of bug expensive:
a748d4a952: No exception, no error in the log. The tool call succeeded, the answer is fluent, and the loop ended on end_turn. The only evidence is a customer who asks again, or first-contact resolution drifting down. That's why the exam treats misrouting as a design problem to be found by measurement, not a runtime error to be caught.
a30e4e4b80: Few-shot examples in the system prompt. They can work. But they add tokens to every request, couple the routing rule to one agent's prompt, and patch a symptom: the tools still read alike. A reasonable second step.
ac09b5fee0: A routing layer (classifier or keyword rules). This is a significant build. It duplicates a decision the model can make, and brings back the brittleness of pre-configured routing (Domain 1). The cause was a weak signal in the text, and a router doesn't fix the text.
f39acab46a: Consolidating the tools. It hides the choice in a parameter and merges two contracts into one description. That's a bigger change than the problem needs. Sometimes it's right (section 11), but it's not the lowest-effort fix.
d44d175e5b: Expanding the descriptions. It addresses the root cause, and costs a few sentences per tool. It's reversible and easy to test. It's the baseline the others must beat.
dab68e6f62:
The new get_customer description removes "order number" from the inputs, which was the overlap itself. It states what comes back, and adds a boundary.

After this edit alone, with the keyword-heavy system prompt unchanged, all five order questions reach lookup_order. In this replay, a strong description outweighs a pushy prompt. That supports the exam's rule of thumb: descriptions first, prompt second. It doesn't make the prompt harmless; section 12 shows when it isn't.
a34e6563a1:
Waiting for dashboards is too slow. The first check is the overlap screen in example 06. It compares every pair of tools on what each says it is and when to use it (boundary sentences excluded). Then it lists the similar pairs that have no cross-reference.

On the case study, BEFORE has 6 pairs with similarity of 0.30 or more, all unguarded (check_refund and process_refund at 0.57, get_customer and lookup_order at 0.34). AFTER v2 has 7 such pairs, and 2 unguarded.

The target isn't zero similarity: order status and order list should share the word "order". The target is zero unguarded pairs, where "guarded" means one description names the other in a do-not-use sentence. The screen is a vocabulary heuristic, so treat its output as pairs to look at.

The second check is the confusion matrix from the evaluation of section 16. It lists the pairs that are actually confused.
b82a8c67d6: Expanding fixes weak descriptions. It doesn't fix two tools that are, in truth, the same job, or one tool that is, in truth, five jobs. Those need structural changes. The two skills in the task statement are exactly these: rename tools and update descriptions to remove overlap, and split generic tools into purpose-specific tools with clear input and output contracts. Use the escalation ladder in this order, and stop when the evaluation says the problem is gone.
2988606227: Rename to make the namespace and the verb explicit, and rewrite the description to match (section 09). It's cheap, but it's a breaking change for everything that names the tool.
769016b06e:
Every pair differs in at least two ways. The consequences are practical:

  • "Manage customer accounts" can't say when to use each action.
  • action is a free string, so the model can pass "delete", and your switch statement is the only guard.
  • The dangerous operation (close) shares a name, a description and an approval prompt with the safe ones.
  • A permission system keyed on tool names can't say "reads are automatic, close needs a supervisor", because there's only one name.
4f74bef68b:
The same shape appears outside telecom. Take a tool called analyze_document that sometimes extracts data points, sometimes summarises, and sometimes checks a claim against a source. That's three contracts:

  • extract_data_points(document_id, fields), returning a typed list;
  • summarize_content(document_id, max_words), returning prose;
  • verify_claim_against_source(claim, document_id), returning a verdict with a supporting quote.

Each has its own inputs, output shape, failure cases and a specific description. That's what "defined input/output contracts" means in the task statement.
11dbc74f65:
The define-tools page advises consolidating related operations. Instead of create_pr, review_pr and merge_pr, it suggests one tool with an action parameter, because fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity. The exam says to split generic tools.

These two pieces of advice apply the same test from opposite ends. The pull request operations consolidate because they share a resource, similar inputs and one permission model, so one description can honestly cover them. manage_account and analyze_document split because their operations differ in contract and risk, so one description can't. If you're unsure, apply the three questions in the figure, then run the evaluation both ways.

The other failure mode is splitting too far. Twelve one-job tools that read alike are no better than one tool that does everything. Separation is the goal, not tool count.
baecfe71b9: The system prompt is part of the context the model reads when it chooses a tool. An instruction that mentions a tool, or uses the words in a tool's name and description, adds to that tool's pull. The task statement calls this "keyword-sensitive instructions". It lists, as a skill, reviewing the system prompt for wording that creates unintended tool associations.
931d62d4ee:
Example 08 takes the redesigned catalogue and three system prompts:

  • the neutral one;
  • the neutral one plus "Always start by looking up the account with account_lookup_by_contact before doing anything else";
  • the neutral one plus a conditional version of the same intent.

Run against the dev set:
641728334b:
In this proxy, the effect on a good catalogue is small: two questions with a clear answer are pulled to the lookup tool. And the proxy models one mechanism only. The direction is what the exam tests. An absolute instruction naming a tool pulls selection toward it. A conditional version of the same intent doesn't.

The magnitude for a real model must be measured. So run the harness of section 16 on the system prompt as well as on the tools. A prompt edit is a routing change.
94983f6634: Suppose "look up the customer first" is a hard business requirement (no refund before identity is verified). Then no wording is strong enough. Prose is advice; a gate is enforcement. The gate lives in the harness, the tool or a hook. The model is told the rule so it can plan around it, not so it can be trusted to follow it:
f912b2f9d9: This is the exam's distinction between probabilistic compliance and programmatic enforcement (task statement 1.4, chapter 03). It matters here because it decides what goes in the prompt. A line such as "refunds require a verified customer; the tool will tell you if something is missing" is fine. It also avoids the sentence that distorts selection: "always call get_customer first".
ed157a595d:
A tool's result is part of its interface, because the next decision is made from it. A bloated result wastes context and hides the fields that matter. An opaque one forces another call. One with no signal for "there is more" or "this was cut" produces confident wrong answers.

The docs' guidance: return only high-signal information, return semantic and stable identifiers rather than opaque internal references, and include only the fields the model needs for its next step. Example 09 compares three styles for listing the orders on an account with 39 orders:
9bdbcead75: Paginate with a cursor and say so (next_cursor, total). A result that silently truncates at 10 teaches the model that there are 10. When you must cut, say so. {"truncated": true, "hint": "Add since=YYYY-MM-DD or pass next_cursor."} costs 25 tokens.
0801576935: One note for later chapters. Long tool outputs are what push a long-running agent toward context limits (Domain 5). The cheapest fix is upstream, in the tool that produced them.
3b3d6bf9eb:
Everything so far assumes a dozen tools. As the number grows, definitions take a growing share of every request. Selection accuracy falls too, because there are more look-alikes.

The Claude docs say that a typical multiserver setup (GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana, Splunk) can consume around 55,000 tokens of definitions before any work starts. They also say that "Claude's ability to pick the right tool degrades once you exceed 30 to 50 available tools". These are the page's own figures, with no methodology given, so read them as orders of magnitude.
372436e378:
The platform's answer is the tool search tool plus defer_loading. You include a tool search tool in the tools array. There are regex and BM25 variants; at the time of writing, the type strings are tool_search_tool_regex_20251119 and tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119. Then you mark tools that shouldn't be in the initial prompt with "defer_loading": true.

Per the docs, every definition is still sent on every request. But deferred ones are excluded from the prompt prefix. They're loaded only when the model finds them by searching names, descriptions, argument names and argument descriptions.

Three rules apply. At least one tool must stay non-deferred (normally the search tool). The docs advise keeping your three to five most-used tools non-deferred. And a deferred tool can't carry cache_control (a 400). Example 14 builds the request for a 112-tool catalogue:
9ba9f1008c:
Design consequences follow.

  • Namespaced names make regex search precise (billing_, refund_).
  • Argument names and descriptions are searched too, so parameter descriptions are retrieval text.
  • Generic tools defeat search, just as they defeat routing.

The docs suggest tool search at ten or more tools, definitions over about 10,000 tokens, falling selection accuracy, or several aggregated MCP servers. They suggest plain definitions below ten tools or about 100 tokens. The twelve-tool catalogue here is below the cost threshold, so it defers nothing.
257f89ddd8: Sometimes an MCP server provides a tool that overlaps with a built-in, such as a custom code search next to the built-in Grep. The model chooses between them by reading the text. If the MCP tool's description is minimal and the built-in's is thorough, the built-in wins, even when yours is better. The fix is the same as everywhere in this chapter. Say what your tool does that the built-in doesn't, in the user's vocabulary, and when to prefer it. Chapter 07 returns to this.
62b5099724: Writing descriptions one tool at a time, from memory, is how BEFORE catalogues get made. A method that works treats the catalogue as one designed artefact, and loops until a measurement says it's done. The steps below are the ones used for the case study. Each is small, and the order matters.
e40bab55e4:
List what users actually ask for, from transcripts or tickets, grouped by intent. The case study has twelve: find an account by contact, read a profile, check one order, list orders, read an invoice, open a dispute, check refund eligibility, issue a refund, check device compatibility, check for an outage, look up a policy, escalate.

The number of tools should be close to the number of jobs. Surplus tools are overlap suspects (the BEFORE catalogue had billing_lookup beside get_invoice). Jobs without a tool get filled by misusing a neighbour.

Then write a contract row for each tool: name, inputs with types and formats, outputs, side effects, reversibility, who may call it, error cases. This is the OpenAPI-first habit. It forces the decisions that prose lets you skip, and it makes splits visible. If you can't fill one row, it's several tools.
1b604e8a4d:
Write the eight parts for every tool in one sitting. Write the boundary sentences last, once you can see the neighbours: a "not for" sentence has to name the sibling that is for it. Use the customers' words from step 1.

Then lint (example 05). The linter checks length, a use-when, a boundary, an input format somewhere, every parameter described, no catch-alls, enums for closed sets, and valid non-generic names. It also validates every input_examples entry against its schema (example 04). On the case study, BEFORE produces 87 findings and AFTER none.
5c0382f37f: Run the dev set (section 16) and read the confusion list. Fix the single largest confusion pair, using the ladder: expand, rename, split. Re-run. Changing five things at once tells you nothing about which one helped. Example 18 replays this on the case study.
b195a648a3:
Keep queries that were written before the edits and not looked at while editing. Run them once per candidate. If dev is much better than holdout, you tuned to the dev wording (example 10).

Put the evaluation in CI. Fail the build when accuracy falls below a floor, or more than a few points from the stored baseline. Most regressions are well-meant edits (example 20).

In production, log the user message, the chosen tool and some outcome signal: the user asked again, the case was escalated, a tool returned not-found at once. Sample the suspicious ones weekly and add them to the dev set. A catalogue evaluated only on queries you imagined at design time drifts away from the ones that arrive.
80731f6dbb: The harness answers one question: for a realistic user message, which tool does the model call first? It doesn't execute tools, which makes it fast, cheap and independent of backend state. A second harness for argument quality (given the right tool, are the arguments right?) is a natural follow-up, and uses the same dataset. The sections below cover selection.
8096aada79: The dataset is the asset. The code around it is a hundred lines. Each row is a user message and an intent label. The catalogue under test supplies the mapping from intent to acceptable tool(s). For example, the BEFORE catalogue accepts either get_invoice or billing_lookup for the invoice intent, because it has two tools for one job. Labelling by intent, not by tool name, is what lets the same dataset evaluate both catalogues and survive renames.
4d78618322: Real phrasings, lifted from transcripts. Imagined ones share the vocabulary of the descriptions you wrote.
22247eae6d: Don't let the dataset leak into the catalogue. If an id from a query appears in a description or an input_examples entry, the model has seen your answer. The companion test test_eval_data_does_not_leak_into_descriptions_or_examples fails the build on that. It's also why the catalogue's example ids (ORD-604211, C-4410) differ from every id in the dataset.
2484a63c15: Sample size. With 48 queries, 89.6% has a 95% interval of roughly 78% to 95%. With 16 queries, 56% spans 33% to 77%. A one-query difference is noise. Telling a three-point improvement from nothing takes several hundred queries. Use the interval to decide how much to read into a number. Use the per-intent and confusion views to decide what to fix, because they're about specific failures, not averages.
03797a05e5:
Runs and cost. A model can pick differently on identical requests. So in live mode, run each query two or three times, and report mean accuracy and stability. A query that picks different tools on different runs is a description problem, even if the majority pick is right.

64 queries times 3 runs is 192 requests, each of about 4,100 definition tokens plus the query. That's roughly 0.8 million input tokens per catalogue, and less with caching on the tools prefix. It's cheap enough for every pull request that touches a description or the prompt.
c6c3847621:
The offline mode in this chapter's companion code uses a deterministic selector, selector.py, instead of a model. Be clear about what it is. It reads the whole definition as text. It weights the name, the first sentence and "use" sentences more than other text. It counts a sentence that opens with "do not use" or "not for" against the tool, for the words it mentions. And it lets conditional system prompt sentences pull less than absolute ones.

It has no semantics. It can't know that "no bars at all" means a signal outage. It's useful for exactly three things:

  • running the harness, linter and gate in CI without a key;
  • seeing the direction of each design effect (boundaries help, absolutes pull);
  • testing the harness itself.

Its absolute numbers are not Claude's numbers. A change that helps the proxy by adding vocabulary can do nothing for a real model. For any decision about a real catalogue, run 11_eval_live.py.
5a87c6a2d9: The live command is ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... python 11_eval_live.py --catalogue after --runs 3 --holdout --out reports/live_after.json. It's shown without output on purpose: this guide doesn't invent numbers for a model it didn't run. The first time you run it on your own catalogue, store the result as your baseline.
9668875d75: The agent handles telecom retail support: accounts, orders, billing, refunds, devices, network status, policy questions and escalation. It has twelve tools that grew by accretion. The numbers in this section come from the companion code (examples 02, 06, 10, 17, 18), using the offline proxy. They show the direction and the method, not what Claude would score.
d3a3d74112:
The system prompt says "Always start by looking up the customer with get_customer before doing anything else." Every anti-pattern in the chapter is present:

  • generic names;
  • one-sentence descriptions;
  • a free-text query everywhere;
  • two billing tools;
  • two refund tools with weak verbs;
  • a catch-all update_ticket that stands in for disputes and escalations;
  • a keyword-heavy prompt.

Lint reports 87 findings. The dev set results:
44035bd057: Thirty-five of the 48 first calls go to just two tools. The magnet is the tool with the loosest description and the most absolute prompt attached. get_customer receives device-compatibility questions, outage questions and order questions alike. That's the exam scenario at 12-tool scale.
b8f5c46234:
The redesign applies the ladder from section 11 to each tool.

  • Rename everything to resource_verb_detail.
  • Split lookup_order (it was both "this order" and "my orders") and update_ticket (a billing dispute and an escalation are different contracts with different consequences).
  • Merge the duplicate billing tools.
  • Type every parameter, replacing the twelve free-text query strings with ids, enums and patterns.
  • Rewrite the descriptions with the eight parts.
  • Reword the system prompt: no absolutes, no tool names.

Then evaluate. The first draft (v1) of the descriptions scored 72.9% on dev. Read its confusion list the way the method says:
78a7619e8f:
The pattern in that list isn't random. The refund tools are drawing queries that belong to the order tool and to the eligibility tool. The fix is targeted, and example 18 prints the diff:

  • For refund_check_eligibility, the purpose sentence gained the customer's own words ("are they eligible, do they qualify, are they still inside the return window").
  • For refund_issue, the "not for" sentence moved the escalation instruction into a boundary ("do not use it for amounts over 500.00 or when the customer asks for a person: use ticket_escalate_to_human"). Now those words count against the tool instead of for it.
  • For order_get_status, the use-when sentence gained "is it out for delivery, why is it still processing".
  • For kb_search_policies, it gained the how-to phrases that were falling through ("how does porting or switching carriers work, how to activate a SIM").
  • For the contact lookup, the parameter description gained a concrete email and phone example.

Result: v2 scores 89.6% on dev.
a89234a40f:
Read it with the caveats of section 16 in mind: a proxy, small sets, and one or two queries are noise. Three things survive anyway.

First, the boundary layer (L3) is the biggest single step, for 840 tokens over twelve tools.

Second, more text is not monotonically better. L4 doesn't beat L3, because the returns and edge-case sentences add vocabulary that makes neighbours look alike. A real model ignores detail better, but every sentence should still earn its place.

Third, the layers that don't help first-call selection (returns, edge cases, examples) aren't useless. They matter for the second decision, the arguments, which this metric doesn't see.
017ef47be2:
The v2 edits were driven by the dev failures. The holdout shows how far they transfer in the proxy: v1 50.0% (8/16, 95% interval 28% to 72%) and v2 56.2% (9/16, 33% to 77%), against 89.6% on dev.

Some holdout misses are vocabulary the proxy can't bridge ("no bars" and "tower" for an outage), where a real model wouldn't fail. Others are real signals that descriptions still share words. The refund pair is still confused, and account_lookup_by_contact still attracts queries that mention "account".

What the case study demonstrates is the method: lint, overlap screen, dev set, confusion list, one targeted fix at a time, holdout once, gate in CI. It doesn't demonstrate a number for Claude. The next step on a real project is 11_eval_live.py with three runs. Then move the holdout misses into dev, write a fresh holdout, and iterate.
072d0069a7: If you've designed APIs with OpenAPI, almost every idea in this chapter has a counterpart you already use. The mapping below helps in two ways. It transfers habits. And it helps you tell the interviewer in the AI engineering loop why an experienced backend architect has an advantage here.
d5bca0232c:
The Spring habit that carries over most directly: the DTO is the contract, and the schema is generated. Define the tool input as a type with its constraints attached. Generate the JSON Schema the model reads from it. Validate incoming calls with the same type. That keeps the three places a field is described (the schema, the validator, the code) from drifting.

Example 15 does it in Python with Pydantic. java/ToolContract.java does it in plain JDK 17, with annotations and reflection, so you can read the whole mechanism without a library:
e5c692e2ce:
Frameworks do this for you. Spring AI, for example, offers annotation-based tool definitions, with a description attribute on the method annotation and on each parameter. It generates the schema from the method signature. The description attribute is the same text this chapter has been writing. Check the Spring AI documentation for the current annotation names and attributes before copying code, because the API is still moving.

Whatever the framework, the discipline is the same. The description attribute is not a comment. It's the routing logic.
4f2a3b0b06:
A snapshot test of the generated tool JSON makes every description change a visible diff. It's the equivalent of an approval test on an OpenAPI document.

A second test runs the selection harness. It loads the TSV dataset and calls a ModelClient wrapper for each row. It asserts aggregate accuracy at or above the stored baseline minus two points, and asserts a per-intent floor. java/SelectionEval.java implements that harness without a test framework, so you can run it directly. In a Spring project it becomes one @SpringBootTest with AssertJ assertions.

Run it against the real model in a nightly job, and against a fake in the unit profile. That's the same split you'd make between a contract test against a real dependency and one against a stub. The static checks (lint, example validation, leakage) need no model, and run on every commit.
bc32009d4e: Each of these comes with the definition, the observable failure and the fix. Overlapping capabilities (section 10) and the pushy system prompt (section 12) have their own traces earlier. The table at the end lists all of them.
a2bb0d4950: A free-text parameter moves the input format out of the schema and into the model's improvisation. The model writes a sentence where an id belongs, the service fails, and you pay for a retry. Fix: typed parameters with a pattern and an example (account_id matching ^C-\d{4,8}$), and one tool per input kind.
7077b3c88a: "Checks refund" and "Process a refund" differ by one verb. The one that moves money isn't marked as such. A message containing "refund" matches both equally, and the first in the list wins ties. Fix: say what each does and what it doesn't, with the side effect first: "Issue a refund for an order. This moves money and cannot be undone. Use only after refund_check_eligibility returned eligible=true."
97393879af: The edit made the description vaguer. It contradicted its own boundary sentence. And it removed the specific phrase ("on hold") that real queries use. In the proxy it costs one query. The point is that nobody reading the diff saw it, and the harness did. Fix: the gate from section 15.
48d68c1e75:
The root cause is in the question: minimal descriptions on tools with similar inputs. The description is the primary selection signal, so expanding it fixes the cause cheaply and testably.

A treats the symptom. It costs tokens on every request and leaves the tools reading alike. C is a larger build that duplicates a decision the model can make, and brings back brittle pre-configured routing. D is heavier than the problem, and merges two contracts.
0590526d68:
The descriptions are already good. So the interference comes from a keyword-sensitive, absolute instruction that names a tool, and the system prompt review is a skill the task statement lists. B fixes the wording. And if verification is a genuine business rule, B moves enforcement into a gate.

A addresses a signal that isn't the problem. C misreads the situation: auto is already the default, and the model is persuaded by the prompt, not forced by the API. D removes a tool the agent needs.
5f33b8f5a7:
The operations differ in inputs, outputs and failure cases, so one description can't carry them. Splitting gives each its own contract and a specific description. It also removes the invented-mode failure, by removing the free string.

A keeps three contracts behind one name. C moves tool documentation into the prompt, away from the tool. D changes the name without changing the problem, and strict would fix malformed strings, not a confused contract.
5cffa842a7:
The tools have different contracts but identical descriptions, so the model has nothing to separate them with. Renaming and rewriting removes the overlap at its source (the task statement's second skill).

A would send exact-id requests to a stale index. C removes the other tool for every request, including those it's right for. D reduces variation but doesn't make the choice correct.
9ce9e71722:
Selection is probabilistic. Five hand-picked conversations say little about real requests, especially the near-miss cases where look-alike tools fail.

A labelled dataset gives a number. Per-intent and confusion views show where it fails. The holdout guards against tuning. And a CI gate catches later regressions.

C measures style, not routing. D measures cost, not correctness: the cheapest catalogue in this chapter (BEFORE) routes 25% of the dev set correctly.
e0fd18a6ca: Add a deliberately bad tool (one sentence, a catch-all data parameter, name run) to the AFTER catalogue, and read the lint findings. Decide which warnings you would make errors in your team.
2320215eb4: Write ten new dev queries from your own telecom support experience (port-in, SIM swap, bill shock), and add them to dataset.jsonl. See whether the catalogue needs a boundary sentence or a thirteenth tool. Don't edit descriptions while looking at your holdout.
d816a022c0: Optional, with an API key: run 11_eval_live.py --catalogue before --runs 3, and the same for after. Compare the live confusion list with the offline one, and record the live numbers as your baseline.
d768dee59f:
Done when you can do four things:

  • explain each of the eight parts of a description, and which decision it serves;
  • reproduce the get_customer misrouting, and fix it by expanding two descriptions;
  • say when a tool should be split, and when the docs' advice to consolidate applies;
  • show that your harness fails the build on a bad description edit.
